analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable standards for immigration detention and phases out private and jail-based detention.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would end the use of for-profit immigration detention facilities within three years, was introduced with 7 Senate sponsors and never received a committee or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set binding health and safety standards for immigration detention facilities, require unannounced annual inspections by an independent watchdog, and fine or shut down facilities that fail. It would end the practice of holding immigrants in for-profit facilities and local jails, requiring all detention to be in government-run facilities within three years. It would also end mandatory detention, create a presumption of release with a judge's hearing within 72 hours of arrest, prohibit detaining children, ban solitary confinement, and require prompt reporting of any death in custody.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants held in DHS custody, their families, and their communities. The bill gives detainees enforceable rights to sue over substandard conditions, requires public reporting of every detention facility and death, and would largely replace detention with community supervision for people who are not flight risks or safety threats. It also ends fees charged to detainees in monitoring programs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires annual unannounced inspections of every detention facility by the DHS Inspector General, with public reports, fines of at least 10% of the contract value for first violations, and contract termination for repeat violations [S3].

Bars DHS from contracting with for-profit operators of detention facilities or alternatives-to-detention programs and requires termination of existing contracts within three years, after which all detention facilities must be owned and operated by the government [S3].

Ends mandatory detention, creating a presumption that a detained immigrant should be released, requiring a hearing before an immigration judge within 72 hours, and prohibiting detention solely because someone cannot pay bond [S3].
Prohibits detaining anyone under 18 in an ICE facility, prohibits solitary confinement, and bars the use of ankle monitors as a condition of release [S3].
Requires notification to Congress within 24 hours of any death in custody, an investigation within 30 days, and a public report within 60 days [S3].
Lets detained individuals injured by violations of the standards sue in federal court for compensatory damages and attorney fees [S3].
Requires monthly public posting of each facility's population, bed counts, average detention stays, and compliance status, and updates to the online detainee locator within 12 hours [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit detention companies and the local jails that house immigrants for DHS would lose federal contracts. The government would bear the cost of building or operating its own facilities and running community-based case management programs. Supporters of current detention policy argue the broader release provisions would allow more people awaiting deportation decisions to live in the community.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison firms and county jails

drawbacks.text: Phasing out all private and jail-based detention in three years would require the government to build, own, and staff replacement capacity, a cost and logistics burden the bill addresses only through a required implementation plan, not funding [S3].

The presumption of release and repeal of mandatory detention would let more people await immigration proceedings outside custody; opponents of similar measures have argued this reduces enforcement and could let people who ultimately lose their cases disappear rather than be removed. The bill attempts to mitigate this by requiring clear-and-convincing evidence to deny release, bond, and monitoring conditions [S3].
The outright ban on solitary confinement applies even in disciplinary situations, with no exception, which corrections officials could object to for safety management [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to people in detention are concrete and enforceable: inspections, public reporting, damage suits, an end to child detention and solitary, and a presumption of release with judicial review. The real costs are the expense and logistics of government taking over detention capacity within three years, and a policy choice to hold far fewer people in custody while they await immigration decisions. The main design weakness is that the phase-out is mandated without an appropriations plan, which in practice would have required follow-up funding legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on April 19, 2023, joined by six original cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents [S1, S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private detention companies and the jails that contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement kept their federal business, and the existing detention system, with its limited inspection and transparency rules, continued unchanged. People held in immigration detention gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private detention firms and the status quo

for.name: Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered six original cosponsors.

for.name: Ed Markey, Elizabeth Warren, Patty Murray, Bernie Sanders, Peter Welch, and Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; none of the cosponsors was a Republican.

for.name: Private prison reform and immigrant rights organizations
for.role: National advocacy groups supporting detention oversight and phase-out legislation
for.what_they_did: Publicly support ending for-profit immigration detention and independent oversight of facilities (the bill codifies American Bar Association detention standards).

against.name: Dick Durbin and the Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Chair, Senate Judiciary Committee (bill's committee of referral)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the 20 months between referral and the end of the Congress; the bill received no committee action.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; no vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: For-profit detention industry
against.role: Private prison and detention facility operators holding ICE contracts
against.what_they_did: Maintain a substantial lobbying operation in Washington to protect federal detention and alternatives-to-detention contracts from phase-out proposals like this one.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Opposition caucus on immigration enforcement policy
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; the caucus generally opposes restricting immigration detention authority.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican signed on, so the bill had no bipartisan support even before it stalled in committee.

industries.note: The bill terminates their federal detention contracts within three years and bans new ones. These companies' revenue depends on ICE bed contracts, and their interest in continuing detention runs directly against detainees' interest in safer conditions and release.

industries.industry: Local and county jails housing detainees for ICE
industries.note: The bill phases out the use of non-DHS facilities, ending the per-bed payments many local governments and jails receive for holding immigration detainees.
The bill bans ankle monitors and other electronic surveillance in alternatives-to-detention programs and prohibits charging detainees fees for monitoring, ending a growing revenue stream.
The bill directs DHS to contract with community-based organizations to run supervision and support services for released immigrants, giving these nonprofits a direct federal funding role.
